content.title: KITCHEN MISTAKES THAT ARE QUIETLY RUINING YOUR 'HEALTHY' MEAL
facts: **Boiling broccoli** – Dumping it in boiling water for 10+ minutes drains most of the vitamin C and sulforaphane straight into the water; steam it for 3-4 minutes instead.
**Salting eggplant too late** – Salting right before cooking does nothing; salt it 20-30 minutes ahead and pat dry so it stops soaking up excess oil.

**Crowding the pan** – Piling too much food in at once traps steam, so vegetables boil in their own moisture instead of browning and lose the caramelized flavor that keeps you reaching for less salt and sauce.
**Tossing the cooking water** – Pasta and vegetable water hold minerals and starch that help sauces cling; pouring it down the drain tosses flavor (and some nutrients) with it.
**Marinating in the wrong container** – Letting acidic marinades sit in metal bowls for hours can react with the metal and strip the dish of flavor compounds; use glass or ceramic instead.
**Peeling everything** – Stripping the skin off cucumbers, apples, and potatoes removes a big chunk of the fiber and antioxidants concentrated right under the surface; scrub and leave it on.

**Cooking oil past its smoke point** – Letting olive oil smoke in a hot pan breaks it down into compounds that taste bitter and lose their heart-healthy benefits; use a higher smoke-point oil for high heat instead.
**Rinsing cooked rice or quinoa** – Rinsing after cooking washes away surface starch along with water-soluble B vitamins; rinse raw grains before cooking, not after.

content.caption:
Let's talk about a few of these in more depth. Broccoli loses a surprising amount of its vitamin C the moment it hits boiling water, because that vitamin is heat-sensitive and water-soluble — it literally leaches out into the pot, which is why a quick steam keeps way more of it intact. Eggplant is another sneaky one: its spongy flesh acts like a sponge for oil the second it hits a hot pan, so salting it ahead of time draws out moisture first and leaves less room for oil to soak in. And that pasta water everyone pours down the drain? It's loaded with starch that helps sauce actually stick to your food instead of sliding off, which means better flavor with less added salt or butter. Everyone's kitchen habits are a little different, so just start swapping one mistake at a time.
